HomeEssentials Inc. - Q2 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeEssentials Inc. Q2 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, participants are required to use the conference ID number followed by the pound key to register for the Q&A session. Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, VP of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeEssentials Inc.'s results for the second quarter. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and David Ramirez, Chief Merchandising Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeEssentials Inc.'s performance for the second quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover five key aspects of our performance:

First, our overall performance showed resilience with comparable store sales growing 4.2% year-over-year, accelerating from the prior quarter and reflecting strength across categories and regions.

Second, we drove meaningful e-commerce growth through omnichannel synergies, with buy online pick up in store now representing 14% to 28% of sales depending on the channel, contributing significant margin uplift.

Third, store performance remained robust, bolstered by remodels, fleet optimization, and traffic gains in key markets like the Sunbelt and Midwest.

Fourth, our marketing initiatives ramped up digital investments with strong returns, while maintaining discipline in traditional channels.

Fifth, supply chain optimization, including new distribution centers and vendor alignments, delivered substantial savings, even as we managed shrink pressures from theft.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the second quarter.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $2.8 billion, a 4.2% increase compared to the same period last year.

Gross margin was 38.5%, primarily driven by supply chain efficiencies, procurement savings, private label expansion, and moderated product cost inflation.

Operating expenses were $612 million, representing 21.9% of revenue.

Net income was $168 million, or $1.35 per share.

We generated $285 million in cash flow from operations.

Inventory levels are currently lean at 10.2 weeks of supply.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

To give you deeper insight, let me expand on these areas, starting with our gross margin performance. Good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report that Q2 gross margin expanded 120 basis points year-over-year to 38.5%, marking our sixth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement and the strongest year-over-year expansion since Q4 2021. This outperformance versus our guidance of flat to up 50 basis points reflects the tangible benefits of our multi-year margin enhancement program, which we've been executing with discipline amid a challenging macro environment.

To provide some context, last year's Q2 gross margin was 37.3%, pressured by elevated ocean freight rates averaging $12,000 per FEU—up 300% from pre-pandemic levels—and aggressive promotional activity to drive comp store sales growth during the inventory destocking phase. This year, we've lapped those headwinds while layering in several tailwinds. Starting with the top line, revenue grew 4.2% to $2.8 billion, with comparable store sales up 4.2%, anchored by a 1.4% increase in traffic and 2.7% in average ticket. Importantly, our average selling price, or ASP, held firm at $52.30, up 50 basis points year-over-year, thanks to targeted pricing actions on core categories like hardlines and appliances, where we avoided the deep discounting seen at peers like Macy's during their clearance cycles.

The largest driver of this 120 basis points expansion—about 70 basis points—came from supply chain and procurement efficiencies. Our new distribution center in Dallas-Fort Worth, which ramped to full capacity in April, reduced inbound transportation costs by 15% in the Sunbelt region, representing 35% of our store footprint. This facility, equipped with automated sortation systems and AI-optimized slotting, has cut fulfillment times by 22% and enabled us to shift more volume from high-cost truckload carriers to rail, saving an incremental $18 million in freight. Nationally, we've realized $45 million in procurement savings through our Vendor Alignment Program, which renegotiated terms with 80% of our top 100 suppliers—similar to Walmart's playbook but tailored to our mid-tier assortment in home furnishings and seasonal goods. Direct product cost inflation moderated to just 1.8% year-over-year, down from 4.2% last quarter, as commodity prices for lumber and steel stabilized post the housing slowdown.

Private label penetration was another key contributor, adding 40 basis points to the expansion. Our Essentials Home brand now accounts for 28% of sales, up from 22% a year ago, with margins 450 basis points above national brands. Products like our new line of modular kitchen storage—launched in 450 stores—delivered 52% gross margins versus 38% for comparable OEM SKUs from Libbey or Rubbermaid. We've rationalized our assortment by 12%, eliminating 15,000 low-velocity SKUs that were dragging productivity, which reduced markdowns by 25% to 8.2% of sales.

Shrink remains a watchful area, but our RFID pilot in 120 high-theft stores across the Southeast cut inventory shrink by 18% to 1.1% of sales, and we're accelerating rollout to 500 doors by year-end. This is critical as organized retail crime continues to pressure the industry—ICSC estimates sector-wide shrink at $112 billion annually.

Regionally, performance varied. The Sunbelt markets, including Texas and Florida with 28% of our store base, saw gross margins expand 180 basis points to 40.2%, fueled by strong comps in outdoor living and HVAC categories amid unseasonably warm weather. Conversely, the Northeast dipped 20 basis points to 36.8% due to a mild spring impacting seasonal apparel and lawn/garden sales, though our store-within-a-store partnerships with brands like Yeti and Traeger mitigated this by driving 15% higher attach rates on high-margin accessories.

Strategically, we're positioning for sustained 100+ basis points annual expansion through 2025. Omnichannel synergies are ramping: Buy Online Pick Up In Store, or BOPIS, now 14% of sales, contributes 200 basis points of margin uplift via reduced shipping costs and store labor efficiencies. We're also investing $150 million in pricing analytics powered by machine learning—think dynamic pricing akin to Amazon's but localized to ZIP-code level competitor data from Tractor Supply and Lowe's. This will optimize everyday low pricing on 60% of our assortment while protecting promotional integrity during peak seasons like back-to-school and holidays.

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 gross margin of 38.7% to 39.1%, implying 90 to 130 basis points year-over-year expansion, subject to potential tariff escalations on Chinese imports, which comprise 22% of our hard goods sourcing. We've already diversified 40% of that exposure to Vietnam and Mexico, but vigilance is key. Overall, this performance underscores our resilience in brick-and-mortar retail, where operational leverage and category discipline are differentiating us from pure-play e-tailers facing 25-30% margins amid rising returns.

Now, turning to marketing and advertising expense trends. Good morning, everyone. As we dive into our financials, I'd like to spend a few minutes on marketing and advertising expenses, which came in at $115 million for the quarter, representing a 12% year-over-year increase, or 4.1% of total net sales—up slightly from 3.8% in Q2 2023. This uptick reflects our deliberate investments in high-ROI channels amid a challenging brick-and-mortar environment marked by softening consumer traffic, elevated inflation in key categories like apparel and home goods, and intensified competition from pure-play e-commerce giants like Amazon and Shein.

To give you a clearer picture, let's break it down by channel. Digital marketing now accounts for 68% of our total spend, up from 55% a year ago and 62% in Q1 2024. This includes $62 million in paid search, social media, and programmatic display—delivering an industry-leading blended ROAS of 4.8x, a 15% improvement sequentially. Performance marketing on Meta platforms and Google Ads drove the lion's share, fueled by our AI-optimized bidding algorithms that dynamically adjust for real-time signals like local foot traffic data from our 1,200+ stores and macroeconomic indicators such as regional unemployment rates.

Traditional media, at 22% of the mix or $25 million, saw a disciplined 8% decline year-over-year as we sunsetted underperforming TV spots on legacy networks like CNN and ESPN, shifting those dollars to connected TV via platforms like The Trade Desk. Print and outdoor advertising, now just 5% at $6 million, continue to rationalize, down 22% year-over-year, with a focus on hyper-local activations in high-density markets like the Southeast U.S.

The remaining 5%, or $6 million, went to experiential and partnership marketing—think in-store events tied to our private-label launches, such as the 'Urban Escape' outdoor furniture line, and collaborations with influencers on TikTok Shop, where we piloted shoppable live streams generating a 3.2x ROAS on a modest $3 million test.

Regionally, our U.S. segment, which represents 72% of sales, absorbed 75% of the spend at $86 million, up 14% year-over-year. This was anchored in Sunbelt states like Texas and Florida, where comp store sales grew 4.3% amid strong migration-driven demand for home essentials. We leaned heavily into geofenced retargeting for drive-time shoppers, integrating Placer.ai footfall data with our CDP to serve personalized SMS offers, boosting same-store AOV by 7% to $128.

In Europe, comprising 18% of sales, expenses rose 9% to $21 million, or 4.8% of regional sales—higher as a percentage due to GDPR-compliant data strategies and fragmented media markets. Inflation-weary consumers in the UK and Germany prompted a pivot to loyalty-driven email and app push notifications via Braze, yielding a 25% uplift in repeat visit rates for our apparel categories. We're monitoring VAT changes and the post-Brexit ad ecosystem closely.

Our Asia-Pacific operations, 10% of sales, saw the most moderated growth at 6% to $8 million, focusing on WeChat Mini Programs and Douyin for urban millennials in Shanghai and Seoul. Here, cultural tailwinds around experiential retail—like K-pop branded pop-ups—drove a 5x ROAS on short-form video.

Strategically, these trends underscore our omnichannel evolution in a brick-and-mortar world. Customer acquisition costs held steady at $22 per new customer, while LTV/CAC ratio improved to 3.9x from 3.5x year-over-year, thanks to attribution modeling that credits in-store conversions to upstream digital touchpoints. We've rolled out Adobe Sensei-powered personalization across our app and in-store digital kiosks, targeting 'lapsed high-value' segments—those with prior AOV over $150—who've been dormant amid economic headwinds.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 marketing expenses at 4.0-4.2% of sales, with continued digital acceleration via our new partnership with DoorDash for 'store-to-door' promotions in 300 pilot locations. This hybrid model not only lifts store traffic by 12-15% in tests but also hedges against e-commerce margin compression. Amid broader industry pressures—like Target's recent comp sales miss and Macy's store optimization—we're positioning HomeEssentials for resilient growth, targeting 5x ROAS enterprise-wide by FYE 2025 through zero-party data from our revamped HomeEssentials Rewards program, now at 28 million members.

Next, let's discuss comparable store sales growth year-over-year. Good morning, everyone. As you know, comparable store sales growth—or comps, as we call it—is a key metric in our industry, measuring year-over-year sales performance from our mature store base, defined as locations open for at least 14 full months, excluding the impact of new store openings, closures, and remodel disruptions. It strips out expansion effects to give a pure read on our underlying health in this brick-and-mortar world, where traffic, conversion, and average unit retail—or AUR—drive the needle.

I'm pleased to report that Q2 comp store sales grew 4.2% year-over-year, marking our fifth straight quarter of positive comps and accelerating from Q1's 2.8%. This came on top of a tough 3.1% comp in Q2 last year, so we're lapping a solid prior period amid a still-choppy macro environment. Excluding the calendar shift from last year's 53rd week in our fiscal calendar, the underlying growth was even stronger at 4.7%. Let me break this down for you across the key drivers, categories, regions, and our strategic levers.

Starting with the comps math: traffic was up 1.4%, reflecting improved footfall from our 'Store as Hub' initiative, which we've rolled out to 180 stores this year—think curbside fulfillment zones and BOPIS bays that boost convenience without cannibalizing in-store sales. Conversion held steady at 28.5%, but AUR rose 2.7%, fueled by targeted pricing optimization using our AI-driven dynamic pricing engine, similar to what we've seen peers like Target deploy successfully. We pulled forward some higher-margin SKUs in kitchen appliances and outdoor living, where consumers are trading up despite inflation pressures hovering around 3-4% on everyday essentials.

By category, performance was broad-based but highlighted pockets of strength. Hardlines—our power category including tools, paint, and lumber—drove the show with +6.1% comps, benefiting from pent-up home improvement demand post a mild winter. This mirrors industry trends we've seen at Home Depot and Lowe's, where DIY projects surged 8-10% in similar categories. Softlines, like bedding and bath textiles, were flat at 0.1%, pressured by softer discretionary spending as households prioritize groceries over linens amid grocery inflation outpacing general CPI. Decor and seasonal posted +4.8%, thanks to our exclusive partnerships with brands like Threshold and Opalhouse analogs, where we saw double-digit growth in outdoor patio sets—up 12%—ahead of peak grilling season.

Regionally, it was a tale of two coasts and a strong heartland. Our Midwest division, with 320 stores, led with +5.6% comps, driven by robust traffic in Chicago and Minneapolis markets from localized promotions tied to home sports leagues—think grilling bundles for Bears and Vikings tailgates. Southeast came in at +4.3%, bolstered by hurricane prep buys in Florida and Georgia, where generator and storage sales spiked 15%. The Northeast was solid at +3.9%, with urban stores in NYC and Boston gaining from back-to-campus traffic. However, the West Coast lagged at +0.2%, hampered by wildfires in California disrupting supply chains and softer traffic in high-rent markets like LA and Seattle, where Amazon and Costco are aggressively undercutting on big-ticket appliances. Excluding West Coast, total comps would have been north of 5%.

Strategically, this performance underscores the payoffs from our three-pillar playbook: omnichannel integration, store fleet optimization, and supply chain resilience. On omnichannel, in-store pickup for online orders now accounts for 22% of comp sales—up from 18% last year—without eroding brick-and-mortar traffic, as our data shows 65% of BOPIS customers add impulse buys at checkout. We've invested $150 million year-to-date in store remodels, adding experiential zones like 'Design Studios' for custom cabinetry consultations, which lifted conversion 3 points in renovated units. Loyalty-wise, our Essentials Rewards program hit 18 million active members, driving 2.5 points of comp lift through personalized offers—think 20% off power tools for high-frequency shoppers—mirroring Dick's Sporting Goods' Scorecard success.

Inventory discipline also played a role: we're down to 8.2 weeks of supply versus 10.1 last year, enabling faster turns and fewer markdowns, which preserved gross margins at 38.4%. Amid port delays and Red Sea disruptions echoing what impacted Walmart's import-heavy categories earlier this year, our nearshoring to Mexico for textiles cut lead times by 25%.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 comps of 3.0% to 4.5%, factoring in easier comps but holiday front-loading risks from inflation-weary consumers. Back-to-school and early Halloween assortments position us well, with 15 new SKUs in licensed kids' decor already testing 10%+ sell-through. We're also monitoring tariff chatter that could hit our Asian-sourced hardlines 10-15%, but our 40% domestic sourcing shields us better than peers.

Now, regarding the impact of shrink and theft on our gross margin. Good morning, everyone. As we dive into our financials, I want to spend some time on a critical line item that's been top-of-mind for the Street: the impact of inventory shrinkage—or 'shrink'—on our gross margin. Shrink, for those less familiar with retail parlance, encompasses all forms of inventory loss, with external theft (shoplifting and organized retail crime, or ORC), internal theft, administrative errors, damage, and vendor discrepancies making up the bucket. In our model, shrink flows directly through cost of goods sold, exerting downward pressure on gross margin, which came in at 38.5% this quarter—up overall but with shrink accounting for roughly 60 basis points of headwind pressure.

To quantify the drag: our total shrink rate clocked in at 1.38% of net sales, or approximately $39 million in lost inventory value on $2.8 billion in quarterly revenue. That's up 25 basis points from 1.13% in Q2 last year and aligns with the National Retail Federation's latest audit, which pegs industry-wide shrink at 1.6% for 2023—a record high driven by the post-pandemic ORC surge. For context, peers like Target reported a 1.5% rate last quarter amid similar headwinds, while Walmart's scale and supply chain rigor kept theirs closer to 1.0%. In our case, high-velocity, high-margin categories bore the brunt: beauty and personal care saw shrink rates exceed 2.5%, contributing 35% of total losses despite representing just 18% of sales. Consumer electronics clocked in at 2.1%, fueled by smash-and-grab incidents. Apparel was more resilient at 0.9%, thanks to lower absolute value per unit.

Trend-wise, we've seen a marked escalation since 2021. Pre-COVID, our shrink hovered around 0.95%—in line with historical norms. The 2022 inflection point, coinciding with relaxed prosecution policies in key markets like California (post-Prop 47) and New York (no-cash-bail reforms), drove a 40% year-over-year spike in ORC. Data from our loss prevention team, cross-referenced with Retail Industry Leaders Association benchmarks, shows ORC now represents 45% of our shrink, up from 25% in 2020. Empty shelf syndrome is real: in high-risk stores, we're experiencing 15-20% out-of-stocks on locked SKUs like protein powders and laundry pods, indirectly hitting comp sales by 50 basis points. Regionally, the pain is uneven—West Coast stores averaged 1.75% shrink, 30% above our national rate, due to fentanyl-fueled smash-and-grabs targeting beauty bays. Midwest and Southeast held steady at 1.1-1.2%, benefiting from stronger local partnerships with district attorneys. Urban density amplifies this: our top 50 metro stores saw 2.0% shrink versus 1.0% in suburban formats.

But we're not standing still—this is where our strategic investments are yielding traction. Over the past 18 months, we've deployed $250 million in shrink-mitigation tech, targeting a 20 basis points reduction in FY24. Key initiatives include AI-powered computer vision rolled out in 850 stores via Eagle Eye Networks and Verkada systems, achieving 92% detection accuracy on theft events. This has curbed external shoplifting by 18% quarter-over-quarter, with real-time alerts cutting average incident value from $450 to $320.

RFID and EAS upgrades feature full-gen3 RFID tagging on 70% of beauty and electronics SKUs, slashing administrative shrink by 12%, while single-use disposable EAS labels on apparel reduce tagging labor by 25%. Locked merchandising includes 100% of high-shrink electronics behind ShopGate smart lockers, and we've piloted BOPIS vaults in 200 California doors, reducing on-shelf exposure by 40% and boosting fulfillment margins by 150 basis points.

ORC task forces collaborate with RILA's Retail Theft Task Force and local PD in 15 high-impact cities—e.g., joint ops in LA recovered $2.1 million in fenced goods last quarter. Internally, our anonymous ethics hotline and AI-driven anomaly detection flagged $8 million in employee shrinkage.

Operationally, we're balancing security with the customer experience: friction audits show spider-wrapped cases add just 7 seconds to basket time, and our 'store mode' app unlocks via geofenced Bluetooth in under 5 seconds. Vendor scorecards penalize non-compliant tagging, passing 3-5 basis points of savings to COGS.

Looking forward, we expect shrink to peak at 1.4% in Q3 amid back-to-school, then trend down to 1.25% by year-end as tech scales. This should deliver 40-50 basis points of gross margin expansion in H2, supporting our guide. Policy tailwinds—like California's Proposition 36—could accelerate this. We're outperforming the NRF's projected 1.4% industry shrink for 2024 through disciplined execution.

Finally, an update on our key strategic initiatives. Thank you, Mike, and good morning, everyone. As we wrap up our Q2 results, I want to provide a detailed update on our key strategic initiatives, which continue to drive sustainable growth amid a challenging macro environment. Retail brick-and-mortar fundamentals remain resilient, but we're navigating headwinds like persistent inflation—now hovering at 3.2% core CPI—persistent labor tightness with wage pressures up 4.5% year-over-year in our sector, and e-commerce encroachment from players like Amazon, whose Prime Day sales grew 8% last quarter. Our omnichannel strategy is yielding results, with brick-and-mortar still accounting for 72% of our total revenue, but digital integration boosting overall comps by 2.3 points.

Let me break this down into our four pillars: Store Fleet Optimization, Omnichannel Acceleration, Supply Chain Resilience, and Sustainability and Customer Loyalty. We've allocated $450 million in capex this year—up 12% from 2023—targeting a 15-18% ROI on these investments, based on our DCF models.

First, Store Fleet Optimization. We've completed 180 remodels in Q2, focusing on high-traffic urban and suburban prototypes similar to Target's small-format stores. These next-gen formats emphasize experiential zones—like dedicated EV charging lounges and in-store demo kitchens for our private-label appliances—driving a 7.2% comp lift in remodeled units versus 2.1% company-wide pre-remodel. Inventory turns improved to 5.8x from 5.2x last year, thanks to dynamic assortment planning using AI-driven tools from SymphonyAI. Regionally, the Southeast is outperforming with 4.5% comps, fueled by population influx in Florida and Georgia, while the Midwest lags at 0.8% due to softer housing starts—down 12% year-over-year per Census Bureau data. We're on track to shutter 25 underperforming locations by year-end, harvesting $35 million in real estate gains to fund 50 new small-box openings in 2025, targeting underserved ZIP codes with median incomes over $75K.

Second, Omnichannel Acceleration. BOPIS and ship-from-store now represent 28% of digital sales—up from 22% last quarter—with fulfillment accuracy at 98.7%, rivaling Walmart's benchmarks. We've rolled out RFID tagging across 65% of our 1,200-store fleet, reducing shrink by 22% to 1.1% of sales, and integrated it with our app for real-time inventory visibility. Partnerships with DoorDash and Instacart have expanded same-day delivery to 85% of stores, generating $120 million in incremental revenue year-to-date, with a 45% gross margin. Technologically, our new edge-computing platform—powered by NVIDIA GPUs—cuts checkout times by 40% via frictionless mobile payments, akin to Kroger's Scan, Bag, Go. In the Northeast, urban density is boosting BOPIS adoption to 35% of digital orders, while West Coast stores benefit from Prop 12-compliant supply chains for higher-margin organics, up 15% year-over-year.

Third, Supply Chain Resilience. Post the 2022 port disruptions, we've localized 40% of our sourcing to North American vendors, slashing lead times from 45 to 22 days and mitigating tariff risks ahead of potential 2025 escalations. Our Memphis DC expansion added 1.2 million sq ft, boosting throughput to 250,000 cases/day with automation from Dematic, improving on-time delivery to 97%. Inventory levels are lean at 10.2 weeks of supply—down from 12.8 weeks—supporting 3.2% gross margin expansion despite commodity inflation in cotton and freight, which rose 6% quarter-over-quarter. Internationally, our 120 Canadian stores saw 5.1% comps, outpacing the U.S. average, thanks to CAD weakening 4% vs. USD, enhancing export margins. We're piloting drone delivery hubs in rural Texas outposts, targeting a 20% cost reduction in last-mile logistics by Q4.

Finally, Sustainability and Customer Loyalty. Our "GreenMax" initiative—mirroring Home Depot's eco-push—has certified 40% of stores to LEED Silver, with solar arrays on 300 rooftops generating 15% of energy needs and cutting utility costs by $18 million annually. We've reformulated 60% of private-label SKUs to sustainable packaging, resonating with millennials who now drive 42% of our traffic per Nielsen data. Loyalty membership hit 28 million active users, with 65% redemption rate on personalized offers via our AI recommendation engine powered by Adobe Sensei, lifting basket size 12% to $52. Regionally, California’s ESG mandates are accelerating adoption, with 8% comp uplift in compliant assortments, while we're countering value-seekers nationwide with "MaxValue" pricing on 5,000 staples, holding market share steady at 14.2% per Kantar.

In summary, these initiatives position us for 4-6% comp growth in FY25, with EBITDA margins expanding to 8.5% from 7.9%. We're prudently managing SG&A at 22.4% of sales through zero-based budgeting, even as marketing spend rises 10% for back-to-school.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to David Ramirez, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines.

David Ramirez, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. This quarter, we launched our Essentials Home modular kitchen storage line, which has seen exceptional sell-through rates exceeding 50% in test stores, delivering 52% gross margins well above category averages. Early customer feedback highlights the convenience and value, with strong uptake in urban and suburban markets. We are excited about the potential of this new product and other upcoming launches in sustainable outdoor living and seasonal decor, which align with our private label push and position us for category dominance.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Instructions for Q&A: Participants may now press star then 1 on their touchtone phone to join the queue. Our first question comes from Alex Rivera with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of inflation on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, Alex. Absolutely. Despite core CPI inflation lingering around 3.2% and grocery inflation outpacing general measures, our Q2 comps of 4.2% demonstrate resilience. Traffic rose 1.4% thanks to our Store as Hub initiatives and localized promotions, while AUR increased 2.7% from AI-optimized pricing on hardlines and appliances. Consumers are trading up selectively in home improvement and decor, mirroring trends at Home Depot and Lowe's, even as softlines faced some pressure. Our Essentials Rewards personalization lifted repeat visits, helping us gain share in a value-conscious environment.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Jordan Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Jordan Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Thanks. What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Good morning, Jordan. For Q3, we expect comparable store sales growth of 3.0% to 4.5%, benefiting from easier year-over-year comps, strong back-to-school positioning, and continued omnichannel lift. We're mindful of potential holiday front-loading from inflation pressures, but new SKUs in kids' decor and seasonal are testing well at 10%+ sell-through. Tariff risks on Asian hardlines are noted, but our 40% domestic sourcing provides a buffer superior to peers.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Taylor Kim with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Taylor Kim (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, Taylor. Certainly. Our Dallas-Fort Worth DC ramp-up cut Sunbelt freight by 15%, saving $18 million, while the Memphis expansion hit 250,000 cases per day with 97% on-time delivery. We've nearshored 40% of sourcing to North America, dropping lead times to 22 days, and Vendor Alignment delivered $45 million in savings. Drone pilots in rural Texas aim for 20% last-mile cuts by Q4. These moves not only supported 120 basis points gross margin expansion but also shielded us from Red Sea issues affecting peers.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Chris Patel with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Chris Patel (Bank of America):
Thanks for taking my question. On shrink, how are the tech investments progressing and any update on ORC partnerships?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Hi Chris. Our $250 million in shrink tech is delivering: AI computer vision in 850 stores cut shoplifting 18% quarter-over-quarter, RFID on 70% of high-risk SKUs reduced admin losses 12%, and smart lockers minimized exposure. RILA task forces recovered $2.1 million in LA alone. We expect 1.4% peak in Q3 trending to 1.25% year-end, unlocking 40-50 basis points margin tailwind. Policy shifts like Prop 36 will help further.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back over to Mike Thompson for closing remarks.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, VP of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
